title: The Most Important Laws You Need to Know for Leading Engineering Teams
author: Gregor Ojstersek and Dr Milan Milanovic
summary: A guest essay arguing that the coordination failures leaders treat as novel were named decades ago, and that the AI era makes them bite faster rather than obsolete. Milanovic works through six laws with incidents from his own twenty years: Conway's, where a monolith could not be modularised until the team was restructured first; Brooks's, where two people leaving an eight-person team cut communication paths from twenty-eight to fifteen and the team finally hit its commitments; Goodhart's, where a colleague who deleted fifteen hundred lines was marked down by a manager counting output, and which now reappears as token-spend leaderboards. Hofstadter's arrives with the ninety-ninety rule and a refusal to give estimates on roadmaps longer than a quarter. Amdahl's is used to explain why AI speedups differ between teams, since coding got faster while approvals, reviews and product decisions did not, so the sequential share caps the gain. Amara's, paired with the Lindy effect, becomes a case for treating innovation as a budget. The closing move is the most useful one: a diagnostic checklist, plus the insistence that no real problem is caused by a single law, so you name the forces and rank them before fixing anything.
points: Anchors each law in a specific failure the author lived through, including a banking monolith that could not be split until the org chart was split first.
Uses communication-path arithmetic and Little's Law to explain why removing people sped a late project up and why work in progress should drop before headcount rises.
Traces Goodhart's law from lines-of-code management to AI token-spend leaderboards, and recommends metrics as proxies rather than targets or rewards.
Applies Amdahl's law to explain unequal AI productivity gains, since the unparallelised approval and review work sets the ceiling regardless of how fast coding becomes.
Closes with a ranked diagnostic checklist and the warning that contradictory laws can both hold in different contexts, so the leader's job is naming forces before fixing them.
quotes: It’s important to realize that a lot of the problems teams face today are not new. We’ve been struggling with coordination, missing deadlines, bad metrics, adopting “shiny new technologies” for quite a while now.
With the speed of building increasing, the bigger bottleneck becomes coordination, communication, and good leadership.
It says that organizations which design systems (in the broad sense used here) are constrained to produce designs which are copies of the communication structures of these organizations.
This is exactly what Brooks’s Law warns us about which states that adding more people to a late project only makes it later.

The main problem with this approach is that when we attach our goals to outputs, people will find a way to gamify these metrics and become good at increasing them, while not actually increasing business value.
For leaders, it is important not only to be right with decisions, but to be right at the right time too. If we miss the timing, then it is the wrong decision.
We should know that no problem involves only one law, but usually a few of them. If our delivery is slow, there are 2 or 3 laws impacting this.
